22990-historical-sketch-of-the-cathedral:
Strasburg Cathedral displays every epoch of Christian architecture in one building, says this Historical Sketch of the Cathedral of Strasburg. For the artist, the cathedral is a subject of serious study. For the inhabitant of Strasburg, it is a venerable monument recalling the principal events of the city's ancient history.

The sketch walks readers through the great church, its famous spire, rose window, and astronomical clock among the wonders. French and German hands both shaped the building, as they fought over the city itself. Guidebooks like this one served the nineteenth century's new tourists, hungry for Gothic facts. Its Strasburg keeps the older spelling and the older pride, stone by stone.
bely-petersburg:
Andrei Bely set his great novel in the capital of Russia on the edge of revolt, and German readers receive it here in translation. A senator's son, drawn to nihilist ideas, is handed a bomb and a deadly task. The city itself feels alive, damp, and hostile.

Bely tells the tale in rhythmic, feverish prose full of sudden images. Father and son circle each other while plots thicken and time runs short. Critics often call the novel Russia's answer to Ulysses. It proved that Russian fiction could be bold, strange, and fully modern in form as well as theme.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-enge:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Engelberg describes a Benedictine house in Switzerland, dedicated to Our Lady of the Angels, at the head of the Nidwalden valley. Blessed Conrad, Count of Seldenburen, founded it in 1082. Its first abbot, Blessed Adelhelm of St. Blasien, received the founder himself as a monk.

Popes and emperors, beginning with Callistus the Second in 1124 and Henry the Fourth, granted the house wide rights. It stood directly under the Holy See until the Swiss Congregation formed in 1602. Engelberg's abbots held near-bishop power over their tenants and dependents, including the town that grew around the abbey walls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adolphus-von-:
Adolphus von Dalberg was Prince-Abbot of Fulda and founder of its university, born on 29 May 1678, who died on 3 November 1737 at Hammelburg. After serving as provost at Zelle in Hanover, he was elected Prince-Abbot of Fulda's Benedictine monastery in 1724. Though not a bishop, Dalberg held quasi-episcopal jurisdiction over abbey territory and held a diocesan synod in 1729.

Dalberg spared no pains to improve Fulda's Catholic education. Its once famous school, hurt in the sixteenth-century religious upheaval, had regained prestige through Jesuits and Benedictines. Hoping to restore the ancient seat of learning, he founded a university, the Alma Adolphina, joining Jesuit and Benedictine schools for philosophy and theology and adding law and medicine. Clement XII chartered it in 1732, Charles VI confirmed it in 1733, and it opened on 19 September 1733, lasting until 1805.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-bra:
Albert of Brandenburg was a cardinal and Elector of the Holy Roman Empire, born in June 1490 and dead in September 1545. By 1509 he held a prebend at Mainz cathedral, and he became Archbishop of Magdeburg in 1513, Archbishop of Mainz in 1514, and a cardinal in 1518. In 1517 he was charged with publishing in Saxony and Brandenburg the indulgence Pope Leo X had issued for building the new St. Peter's in Rome.

Martin Luther protested to Albert over the preaching of Tetzel and over Albert's book of instructions, but his letter was disregarded, and the entry calls the instructions wise and edifying. It paints the young bishop as worldly and extravagant, fond of learned men and artists. Yet it notes that he changed his conduct later in life. As a prince he ruled his electorate well, reforming justice, policing, and commerce, and he became a staunch defender of the Catholic faith in Germany.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-augsburg:
Augsburg is a diocese in the Kingdom of Bavaria in Germany. Under the Archdiocese of Munich-Freising, it covers Swabia and Neuburg with parts of Upper Bavaria and Franconia. Its city appears in Strabo as Damasia, a stronghold of the Licatii. In 14 BC it became the Roman colony of Augusta Vindelicorum, soon prized as an arsenal and trade junction. Christianity likely reached it through soldiers or merchants, and a fourth-century community under Bishop Narcissus is linked to the martyrdom of St Afra.

The church there survived the fall of Roman power and the migrations, though little is certain before St Wikterp, bishop about 739 or 768. Later centuries brought splendor under St Ulrich, whose tomb stands in the Gothic church of St Ulrich and St Afra, built between 1467 and 1594. The entry closes with a survey of churches and abbeys across the diocese, many restored in baroque or rococo style.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bamberg:
Bamberg is an archdiocese in Bavaria, covering most of Upper Franconia plus Nuremberg, Fürth, Ansbach, and Erlangen. Its province also holds the suffragan dioceses of Würzburg, Eichstätt, and Speyer. In 1900 it counted 379,442 Catholics, rising to 410,000 by 1907 against 720,000 of other faiths. Early on, Slavs peopled the region, and Fulda's Benedictine monks brought them Christianity under Würzburg's care.

Emperor Henry II and his wife Kunigunde chose to erect a separate bishopric at Bamberg, a family inheritance. Their aims were to shrink unwieldy Würzburg and to root Christianity firmer in Franconia. After long talks with Würzburg and Eichstätt, the boundaries were set in 1008, with papal confirmation that year. The new cathedral was consecrated on 6 May 1012, and in 1017 Henry founded a Benedictine abbey for training clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baron-joseph-:
Baron Joseph Maria Christoph von Lassberg was a distinguished German antiquary, born at Donaueschingen in 1770, who died in 1855. His father was chief forester to Prince von Fürstenberg, and Lassberg served the prince from 1789, becoming chief forest warden in 1804. As privy councillor from 1806, he traveled Switzerland, Italy, and England with the regent Princess Elizabeth. Retiring in 1817, he lived at Eppishusen, then from 1838 at Castle Meersburg on Lake Constance.

There he devoted himself to German literature, gathering over 12,000 books and 273 manuscripts, including the Hohenems Nibelungenlied codex. After his death the library went to Donaueschingen, and his guests at Meersburg included Uhland, Lachmann, and Schwab. Editing medieval German poems under the name Meister Sepp von Eppishusen, he published the four-volume Liedersaal at St Gall. Its fourth volume first printed the Nibelungen manuscript he owned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-lu: Bernard of Luxemburg, a Dominican theologian and inquisitor, was born at Strassen near Cologne and died at Cologne in 1535. He studied at Cologne, took a degree at Louvain in 1499, and served as prior of Cologne twice. As inquisitor for Cologne, Mainz, and Trier, he defended Catholic teaching against heretics, though his Catalogue of Heretics shows weak critical judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernhard-hein:
Bernhard Heinrich Overberg, a German priest and educator, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born poor at Höckel near Osnabrück in 1754, he died in 1826 after rising from pedlar's son to school reformer. A priest prepared him for college at fifteen, and he studied with the Franciscans at Rheine and at Münster, where he was ordained in 1779.

Good work teaching religion at Everswinkel won him the directorship of Münster's new normal school, a school for training teachers, under Fürstenberg. He trained women teachers in particular, effectively creating the lay woman teacher in Germany, and taught catechism free for twenty-seven years. The entry presents a humble founder of modern teacher training.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-berthold-of-h:
Berthold of Henneberg, Archbishop and Elector of Mainz, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1441, he died in 1504 after study at Erfurt and a canonry at Cologne in 1464. Court service under Emperor Frederick III followed, and he was chosen Archbishop of Mainz in 1484.

As imperial chancellor he won the right to countersign royal documents when Maximilian was elected king in 1486. Heart and soul for reform of the tottering empire, he pressed for a new constitution, a common tax, and a supreme court. The entry presents a prince-bishop who tried to give Germany order before the Reformation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-gertrude-o: Blessed Gertrude of Aldenberg, Premonstratensian abbess, was born about 1227, youngest daughter of Louis VI of Thuringia and St. Elizabeth of Hungary. Her father died travelling toward the Holy Land before her birth, and Elizabeth brought the two-year-old to Aldenberg convent, where Gertrude became a nun. Elected abbess at twenty-one in 1248, she ruled forty-nine years, using her uncle's inheritance for the house.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-brandenburg:
Brandenburg, once an electoral Mark and diocese in Prussia's heart, grew from Slavic lands east of the Elbe won back by German kings. Slav tribes pushed to the Elbe and Saale in the sixth century until Charlemagne checked them. Henry I seized Brennabor and founded the North Mark, and Otto I set up Havelberg and Brandenburg dioceses in 948 under Magdeburg.

A Slav rising in 983 retook both sees and wiped out the young Christian order. Real evangelization waited for Albert of Ballenstadt, made Margrave in 1134, who befriended Prince Pribislav, inherited Brandenburg in 1150, and brought Rhine colonists to drain its swamps. Premonstratensians and Cistercians led the conversion, refounding dioceses, churches, and monasteries, and winning the Wends to church and empire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-centuriators-:
The Centuriators of Magdeburg were a group of Lutheran scholars who gathered at Magdeburg and produced a church history arranged century by century. In 1559 the first three folio volumes appeared at Basle under the title Ecclesiastica Historia, a church history by some learned and pious men of Magdeburg. The name Centuriators stuck because of their century-by-century division and the place where the first five volumes were written. Most later volumes were written at Wismar or elsewhere.

The originator and moving spirit was Matthias Vlacich, latinized Flacius and called Illyricus from his native Istria. Born in 1520, he was kept from becoming a monk by his uncle Baldo Lupertino, an apostate friar. He went to Germany in 1539, studying at Augsburg, Basle, Tübingen, and Wittenberg. The Augsburg Interim of 1547 drew him into the Adiaphoristic controversy, in which he attacked Philip Melanchthon bitterly.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-etien:
Charles Etienne Brasseur de Bourbourg was born at Bourbourg in France in 1814 and died at Nice in 1874. He left France for Canada in 1845, and in 1846 served as vicar-general at Boston. After two winters in Rome searching archives for Spanish American documents, he went to Mexico in 1848 as chaplain of the French Legation. From 1854 he travelled through Central America, reaching Guatemala City in February 1855 and administering the Rabinal district in Vera Paz for a year.

He returned to France in 1857, revisited Tehuantepec, Chiapas, and Guatemala in 1859 and 1860, and joined the French scientific mission to Mexico in 1864. His publications from 1857 to 1871 remain valuable, though the entry warns that early enthusiasm and vivid fancy flawed them. Exhausted by long, arduous, and often dangerous labours, he died at Nice aged sixty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-leo:
Michael Ott's entry follows Conrad of Leonberg, called Leontorius, Cistercian monk and humanist born at Leonberg in 1460, died at Engenthal near Basle after 1520. He took vows at Maulbronn, then enjoying a golden age unlike most Cistercian houses. In 1490 he became his order's general's secretary. As German humanists revived Latin and Greek classics, Conrad, deploring barbarous scholastic Latin, joined their push to restore Ciceronian Latinity.

By word and example he encouraged Greek study, but Reuchlin, Hebrew scholar who died in 1522, drew him most, inspiring his Hebrew enthusiasm. Like Reuchlin, friend and teacher, Conrad held Hebrew necessary for Scripture and ranked among the few great Hebrew scholars of his time. He corresponded with leading writers, highly esteemed by learned men. For a time he proofread at Amerbach's Basle press. Beyond Latin poems, orations, and epistles, he published at Basle in 1506 to 1508 a Latin Bible with Lyra, Burgos, and Thoring additions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-mar:
Johann Peter Kirsch's entry follows Conrad of Marburg, confessor of Saint Elizabeth of Thuringia and papal inquisitor. Born at or near Marburg late in the twelfth century, he died on 30 July 1233. Men of his day called him Magister, proof of a finished course, perhaps at Paris or Bologna. Berthold and Caesarius of Heisterbach mark him likely a secular priest, neither Dominican as Hausrath states nor Franciscan as Henke asserts.

Papal letters and writers of his day credit him with skill, learning, speech gifts, zeal for the faith, and a stern life. He first appears preaching Innocent III's crusade of 1213 with vigor. In 1225, after Rodeger's recall, he became the landgravine's guide and confessor. Even friendly writers found his rule too severe and harsh. First inquisitor named in Germany, he was killed returning to Marburg, and his successor sought harsh justice for his killers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-daniel-bonifa:
A biographical entry presents Daniel Bonifacius von Haneberg, a German prelate and Orientalist born near Kempten in 1816 and dead at Speyer in 1876. At Kempten he mastered Hebrew, Arabic, Syriac, Persian, and Ethiopic with hardly any guidance, then at Munich added Sanskrit and Chinese while studying philosophy and theology. Ordained at Augsburg in 1839, he took a doctorate at Munich the same year.

His thirty-three years lecturing on the Old Testament at Munich made him extraordinary professor of Hebrew in 1841 and ordinary professor in 1844, his learning, discretion, and piety drawing growing audiences. Later he became Bishop of Speyer, touring his diocese until pneumonia, caught on a visitation, ended his life. Clergy and people revered him as a saint, and the entry lists his works and biographers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-david-of-augs:
A biographical entry follows David of Augsburg, a medieval German mystic born probably at Augsburg early in the thirteenth century and dead there on 19 November 1272. Joining the Franciscans probably at Ratisbon, he served as master of novices and wrote his celebrated Formula Novitiorum for their spiritual benefit. In 1246 he and Berthold of Ratisbon inspected the convent of Niedermunster.

From about 1250 David accompanied Berthold on missionary tours, likely preaching himself, and shared in Inquisition proceedings against the Waldenses. Legend says Berthold, preaching far away on David's death day, broke off to quote a hymn for his departed friend. David wrote in Latin and German, and his Latin works were long misattributed to Bernard and Bonaventure, proof of the esteem they commanded.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diether-of-is:
Diether of Isenburg was Archbishop and Elector of Mainz, born about 1412. He studied at Erfurt, where he became rector in 1434, and held canonries at Mainz, Cologne, and Trier while still young. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he sought the see of Trier in 1456 and failed. Three years later he won election to Mainz itself, likely through simony, the buying of church office.

His reign brought the Mainz feud of 1461 to 1463, a bitter quarrel over the archbishopric that drew in princes and popes. The entry follows his quarrels, his deposition, and his later return to power. He died at Aschaffenburg in 1482, a prince of the church whose ambition shaped German politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-friedri:
Franz Friedrich Wilhelm von Furstenberg, born at Herdringen in Westphalia on 7 August 1729 and dead at Munster on 16 September 1810. He was a statesman and educator who rebuilt Munster's schools and government. Tutored privately and by Jesuits at Cologne, he studied law at Cologne, Salzburg, and the Sapienza in Rome, became canon of Munster in 1748 and of Paderborn. He took minor orders without intending priesthood. During the Seven Years' War he served his country as go-between for opposing camps, warding off many calamities from Munster.

After Clemens August died in 1761, Furstenberg's influence secured Maximilian Friedrich as Prince-Bishop of Munster in 1762. The new ruler entrusted him with temporal and spiritual administration, making him privy councillor and minister in 1762 and vicar-general and curator of schools in 1770. Prussian rule after 1803 eroded his power, and he resigned in 1807.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-wilhelm:
Franz Wilhelm, Count von Wartenberg, eldest son of Duke Ferdinand of Bavaria and his morganatic wife Maria Pettenbeckin, was born at Munich on 1 March 1593. He died at Ratisbon on 1 December 1661. He was a bishop and cardinal of the Counter-Reformation. Elected Bishop of Osnabruck on 26 October 1625, he found the faith there in deplorable state, its three previous bishops Protestant.

With Tilly's help he took possession of his see on 12 March 1628, driving out Danish soldiers. Then he pursued Counter-Reformation with zeal: expelling Protestant preachers, restoring churches to Catholics, purging the city council, taking education in hand. He gave the former Augustinian convent to Jesuits as teachers at the Gymnasium Carolinum, restored and founded religious communities, and held synods to enforce Trent's decrees. Driven out by war and the Peace of Westphalia, he kept spiritual jurisdiction, regained Osnabruck on 18 December 1650, and was made cardinal-priest on 5 April 1661.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-freiburg:
Freiburg, a city in Baden at the foot of the Black Forest, anchors a Catholic Encyclopedia entry that covers city, archdiocese, and university together. Founded in 1120 by Conrad of Zähringen, it grew as a market town on both banks of the Dreisam. By the census of December 1905 it held 76,286 people, of whom 53,133 were Catholics.

The city bought its liberties from cash-strapped lords and placed itself under Austria in 1368, sharing Habsburg fortunes for five centuries. Its minster rose from the twelfth century onward, and Archduke Albert founded its university in 1456. Dominicans, Franciscans, and mystics all left marks here, from Albert the Great to Berthold the Black, the friar linked in legend with gunpowder.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-friedrich-pri:
Friedrich of Schwarzenberg, cardinal and prince-archbishop of Prague, was born at Vienna in April 1809 into a princely house touched early by tragedy. When he was a month old his mother fled Napoleon with him to Bohemia. A year later she died with her eldest daughter in a fire at Paris festivities, known only by a gold necklace engraved with her ten children's names.

Raised by his aunt, young Fritz studied law, then told his father he wished to serve God as a priest. He studied theology at Salzburg and Vienna, took his doctorate, and was ordained in 1833. As a cathedral curate he loved parish work, and his rise to Prague's highest see crowned a career shaped by pastoral care and loyalty to Rome.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gerhoh-of-rei:
Gerhoh of Reichersberg, provost and Austin canon, ranked among twelfth-century Germany's finest theologians. Born at Polling, Bavaria, in 1093, he studied at Freising, Mosburg, and Hildesheim, and in 1119 Bishop Hermann of Augsburg made him scholasticus and canon. Adopting a stricter church line, he quit the simoniacal Hermann in 1121 for Raitenbuch monastery, returning with him to the Lateran Council of 1123.

Gerhoh joined Raitenbuch's Austin canons in 1124 with his father and half-brothers, was ordained in 1126, and held Cham parish until Hohenstaufen threats drove him out in 1127. Salzburg's Conrad made him Reichersberg's provost in 1132, sending him often to Rome and, in 1143, to Bohemia and Moravia with Arnold of Brescia. In the disputed election of 1159 he backed Alexander III after long hesitation. He endured imperial hatred, banishment of his archbishop in 1166, and attacks on his monastery before dying on his return in 1169. His writings press Gregorian reform of the clergy through community life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gottfried-von:
Gottfried von Strasburg was one of the greatest of Middle High German epic poets, about whose life nothing is known. Even his poem gives no information, and his birth and death dates cannot be fixed. A Catholic Encyclopedia article dates his Tristan und Isolt about 1210 from an internal clue.

In the eighth book, Hartmann and Wolfram appear as still living, while Reinmar of Hagenau and Heinrich von Veldeke are spoken of as dead. Called Meister rather than Herr, he may have been a burgher, though the title can denote learning, and he certainly knew Latin and French and courtly life. His Tristan, sent by King Marke to woo Isolde, tells how the pair mistakenly drink a love potion. They fall madly in love, until Tristan flees and the poem breaks off.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-graf-von-fran:
Johann Heinrich, Graf von Frankenberg, was Archbishop of Mechlin, Primate of Belgium, and cardinal, born on 18 September 1726 at Gross-Glogau in Silesia, who died at Breda on 11 June 1804. Sole male heir of a family devoted to the Habsburgs, he chose the priesthood young. He studied at Breslau and the German College at Rome, and was ordained in 1749. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a life of every private and public virtue.

Made coadjutor of Görz in 1750 and dean at Prague in 1754, he became Archbishop of Mechlin in 1759. He defended his office's dignity against Austrian ministers who sought Lenten dispensations at their pleasure and meddled in ecclesiastical jurisdiction. Maria Theresa favored him and sought his cardinal's hat in 1778, but Joseph II's Josephinism, the absolute supremacy of the state, changed the situation entirely.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregory-of-he:
Gregory of Heimburg was a humanist and statesman born at Wurzburg in the beginning of the fifteenth century, who died at Tharandt near Dresden in August 1472. About 1430 he took the degree of Doctor of Both Laws at Padua, and, filled with reform ideas, was drawn to the Council of Basle. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows an ardent and eloquent jurist.

At Basle he became secretary to Aeneas Sylvius. He left in 1433 when elected syndic of Nuremberg, and served in that office until 1461. He headed embassies to Eugene IV in 1446 over the deposed archbishops of Cologne and Trier, but his mission failed, and the Concordat of Vienna followed in 1448. Disappointed even by neutrality, he abandoned ecclesiastical politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hamburg:
Hamburg's church story begins with a fishing settlement between Elbe and Alster, fortified by Charlemagne about 805. Louis the Pious raised it in 831 into an archbishopric for all northern missions, under St. Ansgar, Apostle of the North. Driven by Northmen to Bremen, Ansgar joined the two sees, a union Nicholas I ratified in 864. His successors Rimbert and Unni carried the gospel into Denmark and Sweden.

Under Adalbert the Great the see reached its height and its troubles, chronicled by Adam of Bremen. It then sank as Lund became the northern metropolis and the see moved to Bremen in 1223. Commerce and the Hanseatic League then eclipsed church power. The Reformation, welcomed eagerly in 1525, drove the Catholic clergy out by 1528, with the last public Mass in 1529.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harrisburg:
Pennsylvania's Diocese of Harrisburg, established in 1868 from Philadelphia, covers fifteen counties across 8,000 square miles, after Lycoming and Centre went to Altoona in 1901. At its founding some 25,000 Catholics were served by only about twenty priests and as many churches, in a poor farming and mining country.

Jeremiah F. Shanahan, its first bishop, led it slowly from 1868 to 1886, Thomas McGovern followed to 1898, by which time churches had grown to fifty and priests to fifty-five. John Walter Shanahan, the first bishop's brother, took office in 1899. Present figures count 86 priests, 63 churches with resident priests, 36 parish schools with 8,000 pupils, and 57,000 Catholics, including Poles, Slavs, Italians, Greeks, and Lithuanians in the mines.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-heinrich-von-:
Fifteenth-century German poet Heinrich von Laufenberg, a Freiburg priest and later cathedral dean who entered the Knights of St. John in 1445, wrote sermons, verse renderings, and the religious lyrics that secure his fame. His rhymed German Mirror of Human Salvation of 1437 tells Fall and Redemption with Bible stories read as symbols, and a second long rendering glorifies Mary through Old Testament tales.

Both long works were lost when Strasbourg was besieged in 1870, but a metrical German version of a health treatise from 1429 survives. His lyrics matter most: renderings of Latin hymns, original songs of love for Jesus and Mary, and contrafacta that keep folk tunes and diction while pouring a religious spirit into them. Acrostics and artifice mar some original pieces.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-herrad-of-lan:
Herrad of Landsberg was a twelfth-century abbess and author of the Hortus Deliciarum, or Garden of Delights. Born about 1130 to a noble Alsatian family, she entered the convent of Hohenburg in the Vosges at an early age. She became abbess in 1167 and held office until her death in 1195. She began her great work in 1165, within the cloister walls.

The text gathers the sciences studied in her day, including theology, into a compendium meant for the novices of her house. It shows wide reading rather than high originality, and it gives a clear picture of education in twelfth-century cloister schools. Its chief glory lies in its 336 illustrations, many of them symbolic scenes, historical pictures, and portraits of her sisters in religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hohenburg:
Hohenburg, also called Odilienberg or Altitona, was a suppressed nunnery on the most famous of the Vosges mountains in Alsace. St. Odilia founded it about 690 and served as its first abbess. On the eastern slope she built a hospice called Niedermünster, later a convent for ladies of nobility, which lightning destroyed in 1572.

Benedictine nuns first held the house, replaced by canonesses in the eleventh century. Discipline faded, but Abbess Relindis restored it about 1140, and the house grew famed for strict life and learned nuns. Her successor Herrad von Landsperg, abbess from 1167, built two more monasteries on the mountain and wrote the Hortus Deliciarum, a treasury of theology, astronomy, and philosophy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-stras:
Hugh of Strasburg was a theologian of the later thirteenth century, whose birth and death dates are unknown. His fame rests on the Compendium of Theology, or Compendium of Theological Truth, now judged to be his work. For four hundred years it served as a textbook, thanks to its scope, style, and practical arrangement, and it was copied and printed again and again.

The work runs to seven books treating the last four things, grace, the sacraments, the incarnation, the fall, and creation. Few medieval works have been ascribed to so many authors: early printed editions name no author, some name Ulrich of Strasburg, and one index-maker, Thomas Dorinberg, was long mistaken for the author. Recent research has settled the question in Hugh's favour, the entry argues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignaz-heinric:
Ignaz Heinrich von Wessenberg was vicar-general and administrator of Constance, born at Dresden in 1774 and dead at Constance in 1860. He studied at Augsburg, Dillingen, Würzburg, and Vienna. By eighteen he already held canonries at Constance, Augsburg, and Basle, and in 1802, still a subdeacon, he became vicar-general for Prince-Primate Dalberg's Constance diocese. Only in 1812, at thirty-eight, did he take priest's orders.

Wessenberg was, the entry judges, entirely unfit for the post. Wide knowledge notwithstanding, profound scholarship eluded him, and his theological training fell far short. Josephinist and Febronian principles, absorbed in youth, led him to advocate a German national church loosely tied to Rome, state-supported and shielded against papal interference. He aired those views in his 1801 Spirit of the Age and in a monthly review he founded in 1802.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-geiler:
Johann Geiler von Kayserberg, a celebrated German pulpit orator born at Schaffhausen in 1445 and dead at Strasbourg in 1510. He preached to common people at the turn of the sixteenth century. His surname came from Kayserberg, where the grandfather who raised him lived after his father was killed hunting.

Geiler, a secular priest like his friend Wimpheling, educator of Germany, fought church abuses not as Luther would, but by restoring Christian morals in church and state under church doctrine. Where Wimpheling's field was the school, Geiler's was the pulpit, and literary history can fix his place exactly: a voice linking Strasbourg humanists to ordinary hearers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-gutenb:
Johann Gutenberg, inventor of printing with movable type, was born about 1400 at Mainz and died there in 1467 or 1468. Properly Henne Gänsfleisch zur Laden, he took Gutenberg from his father's house, and his patrician family, traced to the thirteenth century, served as retainers of the archbishop's mint.

That mint connection likely gave Gutenberg metal skill: his kin supplied coin metal, changed coin kinds, and sat on forgery trials. His father Friele married Else Wyrich in 1386 and died in 1419. Of Johann's youth little is known, save that he was away from Mainz in 1418, His press, built on mint craft and goldsmith work, remade how books reached the world.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-johann-michae:
Johann Michael Nathanael Feneberg was a Bavarian priest whose parish work at Seeg drew him into suspicion of false mysticism. Born in 1751, he studied at Kaufbeuren and Augsburg, joined the Jesuits in 1770, and was ordained in 1775 after the order was suppressed. He taught at Dillingen, lost his post amid charges of leaning toward the Illuminati, and became pastor of Seeg, where he mapped its villages and took a census of the district.

A fall from his horse cost him a leg, which he bore without an anesthetic. His friendship with the preacher Martin Boos then pulled him into trouble: Boos's followers, called the Awakened Brethren, called Feneberg Nathanael. Church officials seized his papers in 1797 and investigated him and his assistants, and the entry traces how that inquiry shadowed the rest of his pastoral life.
